My point estimates across all three horizons reflect a relatively stable, mean-reverting assumption about the underlying asset, likely a price or index near the 102 level. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 102.0 essentially assumes minimal drift from the current level, as overnight or intraday moves rarely produce large directional shifts absent a major catalyst. At the one-week horizon, the slight uptick to 102.12 reflects a small positive drift assumption, perhaps based on recent momentum or a mild upward trend in the data. At the one-month horizon, the estimate of 102.65 continues that modest positive drift, compounding the weekly assumption over roughly four weeks while still remaining close to the starting value, consistent with the idea that over medium-term horizons, prices tend not to deviate dramatically from recent levels without sustained fundamental pressure.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which follows directly from the standard statistical principle that uncertainty compounds with time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 7.4 points, reflecting normal short-term volatility. By one week, that span grows to about 16.5 points, capturing the accumulation of daily uncertainties over five trading sessions. At one month, the interval stretches to nearly 34 points, reflecting four weeks of compounding uncertainty. The widths were calibrated using an implied or historical volatility estimate, scaled by the square root of time, which is the conventional approach for capturing how unpredictability grows with the forecast horizon.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as a stronger-than-expected economic report, a policy shift from a central bank, or a major corporate announcement — could drive prices well above the upper bound, particularly at the one-month horizon where the market has more time to reprice. On the downside, a risk-off episode triggered by geopolitical events, a financial stability shock, or an unexpected tightening in liquidity conditions could send prices sharply below the lower bound. The one-month interval in particular, while already wide, may still understate tail risk if volatility regimes shift — for instance, if realized volatility spikes well above the historical baseline used in calibration. Fat-tailed distributions in financial markets mean that extreme moves occur more frequently than a normal distribution would suggest, so the true 90% interval in practice may need to be wider than what standard models imply.
